newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israelis mark Rabin death, new political row erupts.
newsitem.headline: Israelis mark Rabin death, new political row erupts.

text.p: More than 100,000 Israelis flocked to the spot where Yitzhak Rabin was killed one year ago as a new political storm erupted, underlining his fragile legacy.

In Tel Aviv on Saturday a 13-storey-high image of the slain prime minister smiled down as young people held out candles in a mourning gesture, allowing wax to drip on to the square where Rabin was shot dead at a peace rally last November 4.

Police sources said between 100,000 and 150,000 people gathered in a tearful atmosphere which contrasted sharply with last year's joyous rally when supporters jubilantly marked Rabin's landmark peace accords with the Palestinians.
But a row over the removal of an army general from Israel's peace negotiating team with the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) demonstrated the tenuousness of Rabin's political testament.
Rabin launched the Oslo peace process.
But Israelis right and left sparred over Likud party Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's dismissal of peace negotiator Major-General Oren Shahor after he met Labour party leader Shimon Peres.

"The meetings between Peres and General Shahor, who is now conducting the most sensitive negotiations, were meant to sabotage the government's efforts to reach peace agreements that are better than the Oslo accords," a Likud party statement said.
Peres, citing Israel's long history of close relations between Israel's political and military relations, blasted Netanyahu for dropping Shahor.
"What is this? Soviet Russia?" Peres told Israel radio. "Its forbidden to meet in an informal setting?"

Israeli-PLO talks on a long delayed Israeli redeployment in Hebron in the West Bank agreed to by Rabin are deadlocked over Netanyahu's insistence the Hebron deal be modified to safeguard 400 Jews in the heart of the city of 100,000 Arabs.
Signs in the Tel Aviv crowd reflected the bitterness felt by left-wing Israelis as peace moves have ground to a halt under Netanyahu, who ousted Rabin's successor, Peres, in May.
"We will not forget and we will not forgive!" said one sign.
"Rabin, only peace will avenge your blood," read another.
Many Israelis on the left accuse Netanyahu, who vigorously opposed Rabin's peace deals while in opposition, of helping create the inciteful atmosphere that precipitated the murder.

"I feel this thing was forgotten too quickly," said Shlomit Shauli, 30 at the rally. "Maybe people here learned a lesson but the people who incited are still inciting and the murderers are running free."
Words from Rabin's last gravelly speech opened the rally on Saturday.
"I believe there is a chance for peace. Your presence here proves that the people really want peace and oppose violence. Violence erodes Israeli society. We must condemn it."
Shortly after uttering those fateful words, Rabin was shot dead by right-wing gunman Yigal Amir, who branded the former war hero a traitor for handing West Bank land to the Palestinians.

"I call on you to pick up the torch that Yitzhak carried and continue to spin the wheels of peace forward. Do not give up on peace because that was his testament," Rabin's widow Leah appealed to the crowd.

In the West Bank village of Husan earlier on Saturday, hundreds of Palestinians were joined by a handful of left-wing Israeli leaders to mourn the killing of an 11-year-old Palestinian boy by a Jewish settler this week.
Nahum Kurman, security chief of Hadar Beitar settlement in the West Bank was charged on Friday with manslaughter after hitting Hilmi Shousha on the head with the butt of his pistol, killing the boy.
